agent_outputs.summary: One CRITICAL hardcoded credential and one HIGH SQL injection, both confirmed by Bandit. The credential is exploitable in under five minutes by anyone who clones the repo.
agent_outputs.top_priority: Rotate and remove the hardcoded AWS secret at config/settings.py:23 immediately.

findings.description: Bandit B105: a hardcoded AWS secret access key is assigned to AWS_SECRET_KEY at config/settings.py:23. It is committed to git history, so rotating the file alone is insufficient. Anyone with read access to the repo can authenticate as this IAM principal.
findings.recommendation: Remove the literal, load it from an environment variable (os.environ['AWS_SECRET_KEY']), rotate the key in IAM now, and purge it from git history with git filter-repo.

findings.description: Bandit B608: SQL is built with an f-string interpolating user_id directly into the query at app/db/queries.py:41. A crafted user_id enables SQL injection — data exfiltration or auth bypass.
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query: cursor.execute('SELECT * FROM accounts WHERE user_id = %s', (user_id,)). Never interpolate request input into SQL.

findings.description: Bandit B324: passwords are hashed with MD5 at app/auth/hashing.py:12. MD5 is fast and unsalted here, so a leaked table is trivially cracked with a rainbow table.
findings.recommendation: Replace with bcrypt or argon2 (passlib.hash.bcrypt) with a per-password salt and an appropriate work factor.

agent_outputs.summary: Configuration is loaded ad hoc across modules, which is how the hardcoded secret slipped in. Centralizing config would prevent a whole class of these.
agent_outputs.top_priority: Introduce a single typed settings module so no module reads raw literals.

findings.description: Secrets and tunables are declared as module-level literals in config/settings.py rather than loaded from the environment. This pattern is why security_1 exists: there is no single choke point that could enforce 'secrets come from the environment'.
findings.recommendation: Adopt a typed settings object (pydantic BaseSettings) that reads every secret from the environment and fails fast if one is missing. Import that object everywhere instead of raw literals.

agent_outputs.summary: One silent failure mode in the payment path that will hide errors in production.

findings.description: charge_customer() at app/services/billing.py:88 wraps the Stripe call in a bare 'except Exception: pass'. A failed charge returns success to the caller, so customers can receive goods without paying and the error never surfaces.
findings.recommendation: Catch the specific stripe.error.StripeError, log it with the customer id, and propagate a failure result so the caller can retry or refuse the order.

discussion_turns.message: ESCALATING architect_1: you rated the config issue MEDIUM, but it is the direct root cause of a CRITICAL. The hardcoded AWS key (security_1) is already in git history. Centralizing config is necessary but does not undo the exposure — the key must be rotated now regardless of refactor timeline.
CONCEDING security_1: agreed, rotation is not blocked on my refactor. Sequence it first. I still recommend the typed settings module so this cannot recur, but it is the follow-up, not the fix.

CONFIRMING security_2: the same file at app/db/queries.py:41 also swallows the DB error one line down, so an injection attempt fails silently server-side. Parameterizing the query fixes both the vulnerability and the observability gap.

consensus_report.executive_summary: This payments service has one emergency: a live AWS secret is committed in the repository and can be used by anyone who clones it. It must be rotated today. Beyond that, a SQL query and password hashing need hardening, and a payment function is silently swallowing failures — meaning failed charges can look successful. None of these require large rewrites; the fixes are well understood and can ship within a day.

findings.description: Hardcoded AWS secret key (Bandit B105), present in git history. Immediately exploitable.
findings.recommendation: Rotate the IAM key now, load from environment, purge from git history.

findings.description: SQL injection via f-string interpolation of user_id (Bandit B608). Confirmed by Code Reviewer to also fail silently.
Bare except in charge_customer() reports failed Stripe charges as success.
findings.recommendation: Catch StripeError specifically, log, and propagate failure.
Switch to bcrypt/argon2 with per-password salt.

findings.description: Ad-hoc config literals; root cause enabling the hardcoded secret.
findings.recommendation: Adopt typed BaseSettings loaded from the environment.

action_plan.title: Rotate the exposed AWS key and remove it from code + git history
Parameterize the accounts query and stop swallowing DB/Stripe errors
Migrate password hashing from MD5 to bcrypt
Introduce a typed settings module so secrets can only come from the environment

conflicts_resolved.reason: The Architect rated the underlying config problem MEDIUM, but Security escalated because it is the root cause of a CRITICAL, already-committed secret. Both are kept: the CRITICAL rotation is sequenced first (locked, veto active), and the Architect's typed-settings refactor becomes the preventive follow-up. The Architect conceded that rotation is not blocked on the refactor.
